scoring: The pot goes to the best hand at the showdown, or to the last player in if everyone else folds. Equal hands split the pot.
Track each player’s net chips.
variations: Jacks or Better: a player needs at least a pair of Jacks to open the betting; otherwise the hand is redealt.
Lowball: the lowest hand wins.
Wild cards (Jokers or deuces) are common in home games.

scorekeeper.hint: Track each player’s net chips won or lost.

games.name: Stud Poker
games.objective: Win the pot with the best five-card poker hand, using a mix of hidden and face-up cards.
setup: Agree the ante and the betting limits. Everyone antes.
Five-Card Stud: deal each player one card face down (the ‘hole card’) and one card face up.
gameplay: Hands rank as in Draw Poker: royal flush, straight flush, four of a kind, full house, flush, straight, three of a kind, two pair, one pair, high card.
After the first face-up card there is a betting round. The player showing the highest face-up card bets first.
Deal a second, third and fourth face-up card to each player still in, with a betting round after each. The player with the best face-up hand bets first each round.
Showdown: players still in turn up their hole cards. The best five-card hand wins.
scoring: The pot goes to the best hand, or to the last player in if everyone else folds. Equal hands split the pot.
Track each player’s net chips.
variations: Seven-Card Stud (more common today): two cards down and one up, then three more up and a last card down, with betting after each round from the third card. Make your best five-card hand from all seven.
Some home games add wild cards.

scorekeeper.hint: Track each player’s net chips won or lost.

games.name: Whiskey Poker
games.objective: Improve your poker hand by swapping cards with a shared ‘widow’ hand, and hold the best hand when play ends.
setup: Everyone puts an agreed ante into the pot.
Deal five cards face down to each player, plus one extra five-card hand (the widow) face down in the middle.
gameplay: Hands rank as in Draw Poker.
Starting left of the dealer, each player in turn may: swap their whole hand for the widow (their old hand is then laid face up as the new widow), pass, or knock.
If everyone passes without taking the widow, it is turned face up.
Once the widow is face up, each player in turn may swap one card or all five cards with the widow, or knock.
A knock signals the end. Every other player gets one more turn, then all hands are shown.
scoring: The best hand at the showdown wins the pot.
Track each player’s net chips.
variations: Some groups add a betting round after the knock, or let the knocker skip their last turn.

scorekeeper.hint: Track each player’s net chips won or lost.

games.name: Pontoon
games.objective: Beat the banker by getting closer to 21 without going over (‘bust’).
setup: Choose a banker. Card values: 2–10 face value, picture cards 10, Ace 1 or 11.
The banker deals one card face down to each player and to themselves. Players look at their card and place a stake.
The banker deals everyone a second face-down card.
gameplay: If the banker has a pontoon (an Ace plus a 10-value card), they show it and collect double stakes from everyone.

Otherwise each player in turn may: Stick (stop, with at least 15 points); Twist (take a free card face up); or Buy (raise the stake by up to the original amount and take a card face down). You can’t buy after twisting.
Going over 21 is bust: hand your cards and stake to the banker.
Five-card trick: five cards totalling 21 or less beat anything except a pontoon.
A pair may be split into two separate hands, each with the original stake.
After all players, the banker turns up their cards and twists or sticks as they choose.
scoring: If the banker busts, they pay every remaining player (double for a pontoon or five-card trick).
Otherwise the banker pays players with a higher total and collects from players with an equal or lower total — the banker wins ties.
Players with a pontoon or five-card trick are paid double. The bank usually passes to a player who makes a pontoon.
variations: Some pay triple for three 7s, or for 21 made with five cards.
Blackjack is the casino relative, where the dealer follows fixed rules.

scorekeeper.hint: Track each player’s net chips won or lost.

games.name: Racing Demon
equipment: One standard 52-card deck per player, each with a different back design
games.objective: Play as many of your cards as possible onto the shared foundations, and be first to empty your ‘demon’ pile.
setup: Each player shuffles their own deck.
Deal 13 cards face down into a pile (the demon) and turn its top card face up.
Deal four cards face up in a row next to it. These are your own tableau.
Hold the rest of your deck as your stock.
gameplay: Everyone plays at once — there are no turns. Start on ‘Go!’.

Aces go to the centre to start foundations, which anyone may build on. Build them up in suit, Ace to King. Only one card goes on at a time — if two players race for the same spot, the first card down counts.
Build on your own tableau downward in alternating colours. You may move sequences between your tableau piles.
The top demon card may be played to a foundation or your tableau. Fill an empty tableau space from your demon.
Turn your stock three cards at a time onto your waste pile, and play the top waste card when you can. Go through the stock as often as you like.
When someone plays their last demon card, they shout ‘Out!’ and everyone stops.
scoring: Sort the centre cards by back design. Each player scores 1 point per card of theirs on the foundations, minus 1 point per card left in their demon.
Play several rounds to an agreed total, e.g. 100.
variations: Some groups subtract 2 per card left in the demon, or give a bonus to the player who called out.
Nerts and Pounce are close relatives with slightly different layouts.

games.name: Beetle
equipment: One six-sided die (one per table for a Beetle Drive)
Paper and a pencil for each player
games.objective: Be the first to draw a complete beetle, one body part per roll.
setup: Each player has paper and a pencil. Decide who rolls first; play passes to the left.
A complete beetle has 13 parts: 1 body, 1 head, 6 legs, 1 tail, 2 feelers and 2 eyes.
gameplay: On your turn, roll the die once and draw the part shown, if you’re allowed to: 6 = body, 5 = head, 4 = a leg, 3 = the tail, 2 = a feeler, 1 = an eye.
You must roll a 6 for the body before you can draw anything else.
Legs, the tail and the head attach to the body. You need the head before you can draw feelers or eyes.
If you roll a part you can’t use yet, or one you already have all of, nothing happens and play passes on.
The first player to finish their beetle shouts ‘Beetle!’.
scoring: The first to complete a beetle wins the round.
Beetle Drive scoring: everyone scores 1 point for each part drawn (13 for a finished beetle). Play several rounds and the highest total wins.
variations: Some versions use a 1 for the head and other mappings — agree the numbers before you start.
In a Beetle Drive, tables of four play rounds, and winners move to the next table.

scorekeeper.hint: Add 1 per beetle part each round (13 for a full beetle).

games.name: Buck Dice
games.objective: Score exactly 15 points by rolling the ‘point’ number.
setup: Each player rolls one die to decide the order of play (highest goes first).
The first player rolls one die. The number shown is the ‘point’ for the whole game.
gameplay: On your turn, roll all three dice. Score 1 point for each die showing the point number.
Keep rolling as long as you score. When a roll scores nothing, your turn ends.
Three of a kind of the point number is a ‘Big Buck’, worth 15 points at once.
Three of a kind of any other number is a ‘Little Buck’, worth 5 points.
You must reach exactly 15. Points that would take you past 15 don’t count.
scoring: Players drop out as they reach exactly 15. The traditional rule is that the last player still in loses (and pays, or buys the next round).
Simpler version: the first player to reach 15 wins.
variations: Some groups pick a new point number each round, or let a Big Buck win outright.

scorekeeper.hint: First to 15 is shown as the winner; traditionally play on to find the loser.

games.name: Craps
games.objective: As the shooter, win by rolling a 7 or 11 straight away, or by repeating your ‘point’ before you roll a 7.
setup: Choose the first shooter. The shooter bets an amount, and other players ‘fade’ (cover) all or part of it.
This describes private (non-casino) craps.
gameplay: The shooter’s first roll is the ‘come-out’ roll.
A 7 or 11 is a ‘natural’: the shooter wins immediately.
A 2, 3 or 12 is ‘craps’: the shooter loses immediately.
Any other total (4, 5, 6, 8, 9 or 10) becomes the shooter’s ‘point’.
The shooter keeps rolling. Rolling the point again wins. Rolling a 7 first loses (‘seven out’).
After a win, the shooter keeps the dice and bets again. After a loss, the dice pass to the left.
scoring: Bets are settled after each decision: win and you collect what you were faded; lose and you pay.
Players often make side bets with each other, e.g. that the shooter will or won’t make their point.
Track each player’s net chips.
variations: Casino (bank) craps uses a table layout with many bet types, such as pass line, don’t pass, come and odds bets.
English Hazard is the older game that craps grew from.

scorekeeper.hint: Track each player’s net chips won or lost.

games.name: Drop Dead
equipment: Pen and paper or the score tracker
games.objective: Score the highest total before all your dice ‘drop dead’.
setup: Decide the order of play. Each player’s turn uses all five dice.
gameplay: Roll all five dice.
If no die shows a 2 or a 5, add up all the dice and add that to your score for the turn.
If any dice show a 2 or a 5, you score nothing for that roll, and those dice are set aside for good.
Roll the remaining dice again, following the same rules.
Keep rolling until all your dice have been set aside. When your last die goes, you ‘drop dead’ and your turn is over.
scoring: Your score is the total of all your scoring rolls.
After everyone has had a turn, the highest score wins. Play several rounds and add them up if you like.

games.name: Indian Dice
games.objective: Roll the best poker-style hand. Ones are wild, and the lowest hand loses.
setup: Decide the order of play.
gameplay: Ones (aces) are wild and can count as any number.
Hands, best first: five of a kind, four of a kind, full house (three plus a pair), three of a kind, two pair, one pair. Straights don’t count.
On your turn you may roll up to three times. After each roll you may set aside any dice and re-roll the rest.
The first player decides how many rolls they use (one, two or three). Every later player may use no more than that number.
Between equal hands, the higher-numbered dice win. Wild ones count as whatever helps most.
scoring: The player with the lowest hand loses the round (traditionally paying, or buying the next round).
A common format is best of three: lose two rounds and you’ve lost the game.
variations: Some groups play with no wild cards, or count straights as in Poker Dice.

scorekeeper.hint: Add 1 to the player with the lowest hand each round.

games.name: Twenty One (dice)
games.objective: Get a total as close to 21 as possible without going over.
setup: Decide the order of play. Each player’s turn uses the single die.
gameplay: On your turn, roll the die as many times as you like, keeping a running total.
Stop whenever you choose. Your total is your score for the round.
If your total goes over 21, you’re bust and out of the round.
scoring: When everyone has played, the highest total of 21 or less wins the round. Ties share the win, or roll off.
Play several rounds and count wins.
variations: Some groups use two dice until the total reaches 14 or more, then one die, to speed things up.
With a ‘dealer’, players only need to beat the dealer’s total, as in Blackjack.

games.name: Aces in the Pot
equipment: Counters or coins — two per player to start
games.objective: Be the last player holding any counters, and win the pot.
setup: Each player starts with two counters. Decide the order of play.
gameplay: On your turn, roll one die for each counter you hold (two dice at most).
For each 1 (ace) rolled, put one counter into the pot in the middle.
For each 6 rolled, pass one counter to the player on your left.
Other numbers do nothing.
A player with no counters skips their turn but stays in the game, because the player on their right may pass them counters.
scoring: When only one player has any counters left, they win everything in the pot.
Track wins over several games.
variations: Some groups start with three counters and roll up to three dice.
In some rules the last player holding counters must roll once more, and a 6 passes the counter on and keeps the game going.

games.name: Aces to the Centre
aliases: Aces to the Centre, Deuces to the Left, Fives to the Right
equipment: Counters or coins — three per player to start
games.objective: Be the last player holding any counters, and win the centre pot.
setup: Each player starts with three counters. Decide the order of play.
gameplay: On your turn, roll the three dice and act on each die:
1 (ace): put a counter in the centre pot.
2 (deuce): pass a counter to the player on your left.
5: pass a counter to the player on your right.
3, 4 and 6 do nothing.
If you have fewer counters than the dice require, give what you have. A player with no counters doesn’t roll, but stays in because a neighbour may pass them counters.
scoring: When only one player has counters left, they win the centre pot.
Track wins over several games.
variations: Many groups roll one die per counter held (up to three) instead of always rolling three.
Left Centre Right is a commercial version with special dice marked L, C and R.

games.name: Four Five Six
games.objective: Beat the banker’s roll with three dice.
setup: Choose a banker, who puts up a bank. Each other player bets against the bank.
gameplay: The banker rolls the three dice until a deciding result comes up. Other rolls don’t count — roll again.
Banker wins all bets with 4-5-6, any three of a kind, or a pair plus a 6.
Banker loses all bets with 1-2-3, or a pair plus a 1.
A pair plus a 2, 3, 4 or 5 sets that odd number as the banker’s ‘point’.

If a point is set, each player in turn rolls until they get a deciding result. 4-5-6, three of a kind, or a point higher than the banker’s wins. 1-2-3 or a lower point loses. An equal point is a tie, with no money changing hands.
scoring: Bets are paid at even money.
Track each player’s net chips. The bank usually passes when the banker loses with 1-2-3, or by agreement.
variations: Cee-lo is a widely played relative with slightly different rules for triples and the passing of the bank.

scorekeeper.hint: Track each player’s net chips won or lost.

games.name: Poker Dice
equipment: Five dice — special poker dice (9, 10, J, Q, K, A) or ordinary six-sided dice
games.objective: Roll the best poker hand with five dice.
setup: Decide the order of play. With ordinary dice, 1 counts as the highest (Ace) and 2–6 as 9, 10, J, Q, K.
gameplay: On your turn, roll all five dice. You may then set aside any dice and re-roll the rest, up to two more times (three rolls in total).
Hands, best first: Five of a kind; Four of a kind; Full house (three plus a pair); Straight (five in sequence); Three of a kind; Two pair; One pair; Nothing (bust).
Equal hands are compared by the higher-ranking dice.
scoring: When everyone has rolled, the best hand wins the round. Ties roll off.
Play for an agreed number of rounds and count wins.
variations: Traditional British pub rules allow only one re-roll (two rolls in total).
Some groups make the first player’s number of rolls the maximum for everyone, as in Indian Dice.

games.name: Klondike (dice)
games.objective: Roll a better hand than the banker. This is a dice game, not the Klondike patience.
setup: Choose a banker. Each other player places a bet against the bank.
gameplay: The banker rolls all five dice once. That is the hand to beat.
Each player in turn rolls all five dice once.
Hands, best first: five of a kind, four of a kind, full house, three of a kind, two pair, one pair. Straights don’t count. Ones rank highest, then sixes down to twos.
To win, a player must beat the banker’s hand. The banker wins all ties.
scoring: Bets are paid at even money.
Track each player’s net chips. Pass the bank round the table after an agreed number of rolls.
variations: Some groups only count pairs or better, so a banker with ‘nothing’ loses to any pair.

scorekeeper.hint: Track each player’s net chips won or lost.

games.name: English Hazard
games.objective: As the caster, roll your ‘main’ or ‘chance’ number in the right order to win. This is the old English ancestor of craps.
setup: Choose the first caster. The caster bets and other players cover the bet.
The caster calls a ‘main’: any number from 5 to 9.
gameplay: The caster rolls two dice. Rolling the main straight away is a ‘nick’ — the caster wins.
Rolling 2 or 3 (‘crabs’) loses.
11 and 12 depend on the main. With a main of 5 or 9, both lose. With 6 or 8, 12 wins and 11 loses. With 7, 11 wins and 12 loses.
Any other total becomes the caster’s ‘chance’.
The caster keeps rolling. Rolling the chance wins. Rolling the main loses.
After a win the caster keeps the dice and bets again. After a loss the dice usually pass to the left (the exact rule varied between gaming houses).
scoring: Bets are settled after each decision. Historically, odds were laid on the chance-vs-main contest.
Track each player’s net chips.
variations: Rules for passing the dice and the odds offered varied from one gaming house to another.

scorekeeper.hint: Track each player’s net chips won or lost.
